subject: biology
title: Passive immunity
key_idea: (Supplement) Passive immunity is short-term protection from antibodies that come from another person. A baby gets them across the placenta and in breast milk. The baby makes no memory cells, so the protection fades and breast-feeding matters.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Immunity is protection against a pathogen. In passive immunity the antibodies are made by someone else and given to you.

items.meaning: A protein that sticks to a pathogen's antigen and helps the body destroy it.
Short-term defence against a pathogen by antibodies acquired from another individual.
A white blood cell that stays in the body and responds quickly if the same pathogen returns.

items: The antibodies come from outside the person's own body.
The protection works straight away, because the antibodies are already made.
It is **short-term**. The antibodies are broken down and are not replaced by the person.
**No memory cells** are produced, so there is no lasting protection.
Passive immunity uses antibodies from another individual.
It is quick but short-term, and no memory cells are made.

sections.heading: How a baby gets passive immunity

blocks.text: (Supplement) A baby has not yet made many antibodies of its own. Its mother passes hers on in two ways.

items: Before birth, antibodies pass from the mother's blood to the fetus **across the placenta**.
After birth, antibodies pass to the baby in **breast milk**.
The baby only gets antibodies to the pathogens that its mother has made antibodies against.
The mother must keep supplying antibodies, because the baby's supply is not renewed on its own.
It supplies antibodies before the baby can make enough of its own.
It gives the baby protection against infection, so it is less likely to catch some diseases.
It also provides the nutrients a baby needs and forms a bond between mother and baby.
Antibodies reach a baby across the placenta and in breast milk.
Breast-feeding gives protection while the baby's own immune system is still developing.

sections.heading: Passive immunity compared with active immunity

blocks.text: (Supplement) Active immunity is gained when your own body makes antibodies, after an infection or a vaccination. The two types differ in several ways.

diagram.alt: A table comparing active immunity with passive immunity. Active immunity makes its own antibodies, makes memory cells and lasts a long time. Passive immunity uses antibodies from another person, makes no memory cells and is short-term.

values: Made by the person's own lymphocytes
Across the placenta, in breast milk or by injection of antibodies
Slower, as the body has to make antibodies
Immediate, as the antibodies are already made

items: Active immunity: own antibodies, memory cells, long-lasting.
Passive immunity: borrowed antibodies, no memory cells, short-lived.

checks.q: (Supplement) State two ways in which a baby can gain passive immunity from its mother.
checks.a: Antibodies cross the placenta before birth. Antibodies are passed in breast milk.

checks.q: (Supplement) Explain why passive immunity is only short-term.
checks.a: No memory cells are produced, and the antibodies from another person are broken down and not replaced.

checks.q: (Supplement) Give one difference between active immunity and passive immunity.
checks.a: Any one from: active immunity makes its own antibodies, but passive immunity uses antibodies from another person; active immunity produces memory cells, but passive immunity does not; active immunity is long-term, but passive immunity is short-term.

worked_example.question: Describe how infants can gain passive immunity.
answer_points: Passive immunity involves antibodies that are acquired from another individual, outside the body.
Antibodies pass from the mother to the infant when breast-feeding.
Antibodies pass from the mother to the fetus across the placenta.
Infants need regular antibodies from the mother to maintain passive immunity.
Infants only get passive immunity to the pathogens for which the mother has antibodies.
